## Status: AI-assisted sketch

The definitions, statements and proofs in this note were drafted by Claude (Fable 5.2) in one conversation with me, starting from my questions.
No human has checked the proofs yet.
The inequalities of Propositions 4 to 6 and Theorem 1 passed a numerical test on 20,000 random finite instances each, and the worked examples were recomputed by the same script.
Propositions 7 and 8 (aggregation without anonymity) are stated with proof sketches only.

**Note:** [PDF, 8 pages](fleet-steerability-note.pdf) · **Source and test script:** [source.zip](source.zip)

## Summary

Abel et al. (2025) call the influence of observations on an agent's actions *plasticity* and define it by a directed-information quantity.
The note asks what the axiomatic approach of Heitzig and Potham (2026) to human power gives for the mirrored question: how well can one overseer steer each of several robots with fixed policies?

The steerability of robot $r$ and the joint steerability of the fleet $\mathcal R$ are

$$S_r=\log_2\sum_{g\in\mathcal G_r}p(g)^\zeta,\qquad S_{\mathcal R}=\log_2\sum_{g\in\mathcal G_{\mathcal R}}p(g)^\zeta,$$

where $p(g)$ is the largest probability with which the overseer can bring about the behaviour goal $g$, $\mathcal G_r$ is a partition of robot $r$'s behaviours, and $\mathcal G_{\mathcal R}$ consists of the conjunctions.
The fleet-level aggregate is

$$F=-\tfrac1\xi\log_2\sum_r 2^{-\xi S_r},\qquad \min_r S_r-\tfrac{\log_2 n}{\xi}\le F\le\min_r S_r .$$

## Main points

- **The power axioms carry over by renaming** and give the same functional forms with the same six parameters.
- **A null axiom contradicts Reliability Preference.** If all open-loop robots must have the same steerability, the exponent must be $\zeta=1$, which the power axioms exclude. For one-shot commands and singleton goals, the $\zeta=1$ measure is the maximal leakage of Issa et al. (2020).
- **Least-robot focus.** Losing one bit of one robot's steerability is uncompensable by $k$ other robots if and only if $k\le 2^\xi-1$. Uncompensability for all fleet sizes forces $F=\min_r S_r$ and gives up strict monotonicity.
- **Granularity.** $F$ is invariant under replacing a group of robots by a representative with their aggregate steerability. No such $F$ is invariant under merging robots into a coalition with joint behaviours. That invariance forces $F=S_{\mathcal R}$, which is a sum for independent robots and violates inequality aversion.
- **Joint versus individual steerability.** $S_{\mathcal R}=\sum_r S_r$ for independently commanded robots and $S_{\mathcal R}\le\sum_r S_r$ under independence. Under a command bottleneck $S_{\mathcal R}$ is much smaller. With shared randomness it can exceed the sum.
- **Human power and steerability.** If the overseer affects the world goals only through the robots, via a deterministic map with at most $m$ joint behaviour cells per world goal, then for $\zeta\ge1$

$$S_{\mathcal R}-\log_2 m\;\le\;I_h\;\le\;S_{\mathcal R}+(\zeta-1)\log_2 m .$$

- **Consequences.** Under independence and $\zeta=1$, human power $I_h$ implies that some robot has $S_r\ge I_h/n$. It implies no lower bound on the least steerable robot or on $F$. In the other direction, a high $F$ gives human power only if the robots are also jointly steerable and their behaviour matters for the world goals.

## Added on 18 November: robot power, targeted steerability, weights

These parts allow a stochastic outcome, with $q_g$ the fleet's own capability for world goal $g$ and $I_{\mathcal R}=\log_2\sum_g q_g^\zeta$ its power as a rational coalition.

- **Triangle inequality in effective numbers, none in bits.** $I_h\le I_{\mathcal R}$ always, and for $\zeta\ge1$

$$|\mathcal B|-2^{I_h}\;\le\;\big(|\mathcal B|-2^{I_{\mathcal R}}\big)+\big(|\mathcal B|-2^{S_{\mathcal R}}\big).$$

  The corresponding inequality in bits fails, because $S_{\mathcal R}$ counts steerable behaviours whether or not the robots' power runs through them.

- **Targeted steerability.** Let $t_g$ be the largest probability with which the overseer can make the fleet behave as it would if it pursued $g$. With the instructable power $L=\log_2\sum_g(q_gt_g)^\zeta$,

$$I_h\;\ge\;L\;=\;I_{\mathcal R}+S^{\mathrm t},\qquad S^{\mathrm t}=\log_2\sum_g w_g\,t_g^\zeta\le 0,\quad w_g\propto q_g^\zeta .$$

  This is a triangle inequality in bits. The uncontrolled power $U=2^{I_{\mathcal R}}-2^{L}$ satisfies $0\le U\le|\mathcal B|-2^{S_{\mathcal R}}$.

- **Without Anonymity of robots**, the fleet aggregate becomes $F=-\tfrac1\xi\log_2\sum_r 2^{-\xi(S_r-\omega_r)}$ with robot-specific offsets $\omega_r$. Unweighted inequality aversion forces equal offsets. If the offset depends on the robot only through its power $I_r$, single-robot composition additivity gives $\omega_r=\kappa I_r$ with one new parameter $\kappa\ge0$.
- **The two constructions agree.** The anonymous aggregate of the targeted steerabilities $S^{\mathrm t}_r=L_r-I_r$ is the case $\kappa=1$ with $S_r$ replaced by $L_r$. A robot whose behaviour does not affect the goals then has $S^{\mathrm t}_r=0$ and no longer lowers the fleet value.

## Limitations

The overseer is fully rational and capabilities are undiscounted.
With a boundedly rational overseer both bounds on $I_h$ can fail.
Direct effects of the overseer on the world and aggregation over time are not treated.
The targeted steerability is a ratio, so a one-bit gap counts the same for a weak and a strong robot; an aggregate of the absolute uncontrolled powers is an alternative that the axioms do not decide.
How one robot's capability in a fleet depends on the assumed behaviour of the others is left open.
